message:
Depend on the published flyte_core, and publish flyte (#4)

flyte_core 0.1.0 is on crates.io (flyteorg/flyte-sdk#1408), so the git-rev
dependency that made this crate unpublishable can become a version requirement.
`cargo publish --dry-run -p flyte` now succeeds; on main it fails with "all
dependencies must have a version requirement specified when publishing".

flyteidl2 moves to =2.0.40 in the same commit, not as a follow-up. flyte_core
pins it with `=`, this workspace pins it with `=`, and the two crates pass
flyteidl2 types across the API boundary -- so two different exact requirements
do not merely conflict, they are unresolvable. They have to move together.

Both crates now publish as a single `cargo publish -p flyte-macros -p flyte`
rather than two commands. Cargo orders them by dependency and waits for each to
reach the index before starting the next, and -- the reason this matters --
dry-running `flyte` on its own cannot work for a first release, because it looks
for a `flyte-macros` that is not on the registry yet. That would have blocked
the release at the verify step. Needs cargo 1.90+ for workspace publishing.

Note the worker still embeds libpython: flyte_core's default features include
pyo3/auto-initialize, which is what this crate wants today since the worker
hosts an interpreter. That ends with the pure-Rust controller swap.

Verified: cargo build/test/clippy all clean against the registry crate, and the
batched dry-run uploads both crates (aborting only for the dry run).

Co-authored-by: Ketan Umare <kumare3@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Release flyteplugins-rs 0.0.2

Launcher-side changes since 0.0.1: the descriptor is found automatically so
`fallback_descriptor` is no longer needed, `dockerfile=` and `image_name=` allow
a worker image the layer DSL cannot express, and `find_binary` searches the
enclosing workspace rather than only the crate.

Nothing under crates/ changed since rs-v0.1.0, so there is no matching Rust
release — the two halves are versioned independently and coupled by the
descriptor contract, not by matching numbers.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

README: OSS-ready

Experimental warning up top, then only what a user needs: the example, run
locally via flyte::run in a test, run remotely via `flyte run` (with the
remote image builder config), compose from a Python workflow, build from
source, status. Internal cluster references, smoke-test walkthrough, worker
contract, and architecture notes removed — the example directory keeps the
developer detail.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add PyPI and crates.io release workflows (#2)

Two independent release trains, tagged `py-v*` and `rs-v*`.

The packages are deliberately not version-locked. What couples the launcher to
the worker is the descriptor contract (`flyte_interface_version`), which is
already explicit and checked at runtime with a clear error naming both sides.
Matching version numbers would add nothing on top of that check while forcing
empty releases on whichever half did not change. docs/releasing.md records the
reasoning, including the one unversioned contract (the worker's argument list)
that should be treated as a descriptor bump when it changes.

release-python.yml lints, builds sdist + wheel, checks the tag against
pyproject.toml, asserts rust.dockerignore is inside both artifacts, installs the
wheel into a clean venv and imports it, then uploads via PyPI Trusted Publishing
(no stored token). The dockerignore assertion guards the regression fixed in #1:
that file is force-included and is not a .py file, so packaging changes can drop
it silently, and a wheel without it means multi-GB contexts and a rebuild per
run.

release-rust.yml runs clippy and the test suite, checks the tag against the
workspace version, dry-run publishes both crates, then publishes flyte-macros
before flyte.

Publishing prerequisites, all verified with `cargo publish --dry-run`:
- add `repository` metadata to both crates;
- give the `flyte-macros` path dependency a version requirement, since crates.io
  strips `path` and resolves from the registry.

`flyte` still cannot publish: `flyte_core` is a git dependency and crates.io
rejects those. The dry-run step fails with that exact error rather than letting
a tag imply a release that cannot ship. `flyte-macros` publishes cleanly today.

Also pin a ruff config (line-length 100, matching how the package is actually
written) so local and CI agree instead of rewrapping hand-tuned signatures to
the 88-column default, and fix the three lint errors this leaves. Verified the
lint fixes are image-tag-neutral; the tag does change in this commit, but from
the Cargo manifest edits, which are genuine build inputs.

No `cargo fmt --check` gate: the tree is not rustfmt-clean and a release should
not block on style. That belongs in PR CI, once the tree is formatted.

Co-authored-by: Ketan Umare <kumare3@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

flyte::condition: wait for an external signal

A task can now pause for something outside it -- a human approving a deploy, a
system calling back -- and resume with the value it was signalled with.

Creating and waiting are separate, which is the point: create() registers the
condition, so it is visible and answerable from that moment, and wait()
collects the answer later. The human-approval example raises two reviews up
front so reviewers work in parallel, then try_join!s their answers.

- ConditionValue is sealed to bool/i64/i32/f64/f32/String, so waiting on a
  FlyteStruct is a compile error rather than a run that fails when someone tries
  to answer it. Decoding reuses FlyteType::from_literal.
- The value type is pinned at create() because the declared LiteralType is part
  of the registration payload -- the backend validates a signal against it and
  the CLI formats one from it.
- Action names reuse hash::sub_action_name and the Sequencer, passing the
  condition name as both identity and inputs hash exactly as Python does, so
  names match across SDKs and a retry finds an already-signalled condition
  instead of asking again. A reused name warns: unlike identical traces, two
  same-named conditions are two questions a person answers separately.
- Error::Condition carries a ConditionOutcome (TimedOut/Failed/Aborted/Unknown)
  so callers can match on the outcome, and worker.rs reports it as a USER error
  with Python's codes -- a rejected approval is not a system fault, and would
  otherwise get the wrong retry semantics. Error is now #[non_exhaustive], which
  is cheap while the SDK is experimental.
- Recovered counts as success when reading the value: the condition was adopted
  from a prior run and its answer is valid.
- create() outside a task context fails immediately rather than handing back a
  handle that can never resolve.

Verified: 28 tests pass, the example declares correctly through
flyteplugins-rs, and the CLI derives --version from the Rust signature. The
live round trip (pause, `flyte signal condition`, resume) is untested.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: design for flyte::condition, plus known gaps

Design only — no code. Waiting on an external signal needs six additive edits
in rs_controller, which lives in the flyte-sdk repo and is not yet agreed, so
this records the design rather than half-building it.

Named `condition` to match the Python SDK and to avoid reading as Unix signal
handling (tokio::signal). flyteidl2 2.0.37 already generates everything needed
and the backend is shipped, so the work is plumbing: rs_controller's
merge_update reads output_uri but never ActionUpdate.value, which is where a
signalled payload arrives.

Two things fall out for free: submit_action is already "enqueue then block
until terminal" and Paused is not terminal, so it IS the wait; and Python
derives a condition's action name with the same md5/base36 scheme we
implement, so hash::sub_action_name and Sequencer are reusable and the
cross-language goldens are computed here.

Records the wire details that are easy to get wrong (inputs_uri placeholder
that is never written but must be non-empty, Unspecified rather than Succeeded
local phase, RECOVERED as success-equivalent), the cancel-safety limit (a
dropped wait leaks a PAUSED action because cancel_action never calls Abort),
and why the trace naming analogy does not extend to conditions.

Second section records other verified gaps: fasttask, the native launcher, the
two upstream image-IDL fixes, and single-stage build caching.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Stop hashing 5.3GB of dead sources on every `flyte run`

`flyte run examples/human-approval/task.py` spent 11.7s of a 13.9s startup
inside `Image._get_hash_digest()`, reading every file under
`../flyte-sdk/rs_controller/target/` before it could ask the registry whether
the image already existed.

Two independent causes, both fixed here.

The ignore file was a no-op for the tag hash. The SDK consumes the ignore list
through two paths, and only one accepts an arbitrary filename: the build-context
upload reads the DockerIgnore layer's path directly, but `_get_hash_digest`
builds a `DockerfileIgnore(<dir of that path>)`, and that class loads only
`<dir>/.dockerignore` and only matches paths underneath `<dir>`. Our
`rust.dockerignore`, shipped inside the package, failed both conditions, so its
matcher was None and nothing was excluded -- not `target/`, and not `*.py`
either. That second omission meant editing `task.py` or refreshing
`interface_gen.py` changed the image tag and forced a full remote Rust rebuild.

Add `/.dockerignore` at the workspace root -- the one name and location the hash
honours -- and prefer it over the packaged copy, which stays as a template.

`rs_controller` was also already dead weight. 170eabe moved `flyte_core` to a
git dependency, so nothing path-depends on that checkout; cargo never looked at
the 5.3GB being hashed and uploaded. Drop it from the image layers, the task
plumbing, all four example launchers, docker/Dockerfile and build-image.sh.

Add two warnings so this cannot stall silently again: one when no usable root
`.dockerignore` is found, one naming any copied folder whose `target/` the hash
will walk regardless.

Warm `flyte run`: 15.15s -> 1.76s (tag hash 11.72s -> 0.004s, local CPU
9.2s -> 0.56s). Verified across all four examples that `.rs` edits still change
the tag and `.py` edits no longer do, and that the worker image builds without
the rs_controller context.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Depend on flyte_core via git instead of a sibling checkout

flyteorg/flyte-sdk#1401 is merged, so pin flyte_core to that commit and drop the
requirement to clone flyte-sdk next door just to build. Publishing to crates.io
would be the tidier answer but flyte_core is not published and its manifest lacks
the description/license cargo requires -- and the dependency disappears entirely
with the pure-Rust controller swap, so a git pin is the right amount of effort.

Pinned by rev for reproducibility. Verified by renaming the sibling checkout away
and rebuilding flyte_core and flyte from scratch: it compiles from the git source
and all 28 tests pass.

Note this means the SDK cannot itself be published to crates.io until flyte_core
is, since crates.io rejects git dependencies.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Rename the generated descriptor and shrink it

interface_gen.py said "GENERATED ... do not edit" in a seven-line docstring
wrapping one line of data, and the name gave no hint it was disposable.

It is now _generated_interface.py, leading underscore and all, carrying
three comment lines that answer the two questions someone actually has on
finding it: it is generated, and deleting it is fine because any launch with
a built binary writes it back. What it no longer says is "do not edit",
which was never the useful warning -- edits are overwritten, not honoured.

No fallback for the old name: nothing is using this yet, so the rename is
free. A crate carrying only interface_gen.py would fail with the same
message any crate missing its descriptor gets, which names the fix.

A root ruff.toml excludes the generated file from formatting. CI lints only
python/flyteplugins-rs so this was not breaking anything, but the file is
written single-line and reflowing it locally starts a fight with the
generator that the generator always wins.

flyteplugins-rs 0.0.3.

Support more than one action per container

Everything a reusable container needs from the SDK, plus the launcher half
that declares one. The worker half is a separate crate in a separate repo,
unionai/union-reuse; nothing here depends on it.

  context: a task-local CURRENT alongside the process-global, so concurrent
  actions stop sharing an action_name, run_base_dir and trace sequencer.
  current() prefers the task-local, so the one-shot path is unchanged. Adds
  flyte::spawn, because both CURRENT and IN_TRACE are task-locals and a bare
  tokio::spawn drops them -- traced steps in the spawned future would run
  un-recorded. Same-task combinators were never affected.

  controller: Controller::for_run, sharing one connection, worker pool and
  informer cache across runs. flyte_core keys its informer cache by
  "{run_name}.{parent_action}", so one CoreBaseController already
  multiplexes runs -- verified before relying on it.

  storage: Clone, sharing the per-scheme client cache. A replica builds its
  S3/GCS clients once instead of per action, and credential resolution is
  not cheap.

  worker: the entrypoint split into parts a second entrypoint can reuse.
  resolve_config_with_env takes an env lookup, because a reusable container
  cannot read identity from process env -- the pod's variables are fixed when
  the replica starts and name whichever action came first, so per-action
  identity arrives in-band instead. init_process_env separates what is
  genuinely process-scoped, since set_var is unsound once a second thread
  exists.

  flyteplugins-rs: rust_task(reuse=...) emits the actor task type and the
  ExecutionEnv blob the fasttask plugin reads, and the image gets a second
  name for its binary -- a replica is launched as unionai-actor-bridge, not
  with the task's own args. The environment identity hash comes from the
  Python SDK's own helper rather than a reimplementation, so Rust and Python
  pools agree on what forces a new pool.

Verified end to end on a real backend: two runs, two actions, one process
(the example reports "action #1" then "action #2" from a process-global
counter, which can only happen if the second action ran in the first
action's process).

Version bumped to 0.1.1: union-reuse pins these additions with =, so they
have to reach crates.io before it can publish.

Support task groups: flyte::group(name, fut)

The Rust equivalent of Python's `with flyte.group(name):`. Traces and
conditions started inside the future carry the group to the backend, and
the group is folded into both their call-sequence key and their action name
exactly as Python does (`-{group}` suffix; `{key}:{group}`), so names stay
byte-compatible and identical calls in different groups don't share a
counter. Groups replace rather than nest, and flyte::spawn carries them.

Pinned with a golden value from Python's new_sub_action_from.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Examples depend on the published flyte crate (#5)

With `flyte` 0.1.0 on crates.io, the examples can be what a user would actually
write. Each manifest now says `flyte = "0.1"` with literal versions instead of
workspace inheritance and a path dependency, and each task.py has lost its last
repo-specific argument. A user can copy an example directory out of the tree and
it builds.

That standalone property is not cosmetic -- it is what lets the worker image
build from the example directory alone rather than from a copy of the whole
workspace, which is smaller, faster, and no longer perturbed by unrelated crates.

`[patch.crates-io]` in the root manifest keeps the dev loop honest: in-workspace
builds redirect `flyte` to crates/flyte, so `cargo build` and `cargo test` still
exercise the working tree even though the manifests name a released version. The
patch does not apply when the directory is built on its own, which is exactly the
distinction wanted.

Two things had to be fixed for the crate-only context to be correct:

find_binary now walks up from the crate instead of looking in one fixed place.
Dropping `workspace=` moved the search to crate_dir/target, but a workspace
member builds into the *workspace root's* target/ -- so the binary was never
found, and every example silently fell back to its bundled interface_gen.py.
That would have quietly given up the guarantee that the Rust signature is what
gets launched: a renamed parameter would no longer be caught. The walk is
bounded at the enclosing repository so a miss cannot match an unrelated binary
somewhere up the filesystem. Verified the refresh works by corrupting a bundled
descriptor and watching it get rewritten from the binary.

Each example also gets its own .dockerignore. The build-context root moved from
the workspace to the crate, and the SDK's tag hash only honours an ignore file
named .dockerignore at that root -- without one, editing task.py would mint a new
image tag and rebuild the worker on every run.

Verified: cargo build/test/clippy clean; a standalone copy of an example builds
against the registry crate; all four launchers resolve their interface from the
binary with no warnings; editing task.py, interface_gen.py or a README leaves the
tag alone while editing main.rs or Cargo.toml changes it; and `flyte run
examples/hello-trace/task.py my_task --x 21 --label demo` reaches
ACTION_PHASE_SUCCEEDED with the image built from the crate directory alone.

Signed-off-by: debasisdwivedy <debasisdwivedy@DD-MSI.tail572d57.ts.net>

Find the descriptor automatically, and allow a Dockerfile (#6)

Two things every launcher had to say that it should not have had to.

`fallback_descriptor=interface_gen.DESCRIPTOR` was pure ceremony: the generated
module always sits beside the crate under a fixed name, so the launcher can find
it. It is now optional, and passing it means "use this instead of the one beside
the crate" rather than "here is the obvious one". With `import interface_gen`
also gone, a launcher is down to crate_dir and binary.

The import mattered for a reason that is easy to miss, and the replacement keeps
it: `--copy-style loaded_modules` bundles the modules a launch *loaded*, so a
descriptor merely read as text would never reach the container and the task would
have no interface there. Loading it through importlib and registering it in
sys.modules keeps it in the bundle -- verified against the SDK's own file lister,
not assumed. The module name is namespaced per crate, because a Python workflow
can pull in several Rust tasks and every crate names its generated module the
same thing.

With no fallback to fall back to, a crate that has neither a built binary nor a
generated module now gets an error saying to run cargo build once and commit the
result, rather than a TypeError about a missing argument.

`dockerfile=` covers what declarative layers cannot express: a private base
image, system packages in the runtime stage, or a multi-stage build that keeps
the Rust toolchain out of the shipped image. The new custom-image example is a
real one -- it shells out to git, which no layer would put in the runtime stage,
so the task only runs if the image was built from its Dockerfile. Built and run
under docker: the binary starts (so the libpython contract holds), git is
present, and multi-stage takes the image to 230MB against a ~1.5GB toolchain
base.

Guard rails, because each of these fails confusingly otherwise: from_dockerfile
has no registry to inherit, so a missing one is caught with an actionable
message; a nonexistent path is caught before the build; and workspace= with
dockerfile= is rejected rather than silently ignored, since a Dockerfile brings
its own context and the workspace copying would simply not happen.

The image tag is unchanged, so none of this triggers a rebuild.

Add the reusable example

A task that runs in a warm container: the backend keeps a pool of replicas
alive and streams actions to them instead of scheduling a pod each time.

The Rust side is one dependency and one changed attribute -- union-reuse,
and #[union_reuse::main] in place of #[flyte::main]. The launch side is
reuse=flyte.ReusePolicy(...). Everything else is what it always was.

The image is still declarative layers built by the remote builder, so this
needs no docker: reuse= only adds the second name a pool replica is
launched under, since the plugin replaces the container's args with
`unionai-actor-bridge ...` rather than using the task's own.

The example reports which action it is on its replica, from a process
counter. A one-shot container says #1 forever; a warm one counts up, which
is the whole observable difference. workflow.py adds a Python parent that
fans out to it -- deliberately not reusable itself, because a parent that
waits on children would hold a slot for its whole life and starve them.

Verified on a live backend with the remote builder: "11^2 = 121 (action #1
on this replica)".

Document the trace-naming guarantee accurately

The concurrent-traces example claimed identical concurrent inputs "won't replay
reliably". That overstated things in both directions, so correct the record
where the code lives:

- Calls with distinct inputs never share a counter (the key is
  identity + inputs hash), so each gets seq 1 and its name is a pure function
  of the call — already independent of completion order. No race exists there.
- Calls that do share a counter are byte-identical and interchangeable, so
  drawing sequence numbers in arrival order is immaterial.
- The one real consequence: if the number of identical calls differs between
  attempts, the surplus re-runs. A missed replay, never a wrong result.

Also note on sub_action_name why seq cannot be dropped even though inputs
already disambiguate: it keeps N repeated identical calls as N steps rather
than one memoized action, and it is part of Python's component string, so
removing it would diverge from Python's names (sub_action_name_matches_python
pins that).

No behavior change. Two tests pin the property: reversing arrival order over
distinct inputs yields identical names, and repeated identical inputs advance
the shared counter.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

docs: conditions create and wait separately, and rs_controller is done

Correcting a design error: I had the API registering the condition lazily at
wait(). That is wrong. Creating a condition is what makes it exist — it becomes
visible for a human to answer and its webhook fires — so create() and wait()
must be separate, as they are in Python. A task can then raise several
questions up front, do other work, and collect the answers later, possibly from
different code. The value type is pinned at create() because the declared
LiteralType is part of the registration payload.

The rs_controller half is now implemented and up as flyteorg/flyte-sdk#1401, so
the change list becomes a summary of what shipped rather than a blocker. That
included one thing the earlier design had explicitly dismissed: submit_action
had to be split into start_action + wait_for_action, since decoupling requires a
wait that can be claimed by a caller that did not submit the action.

Also drops the now-false claim that submit_action needed no change, and makes
Recovered concrete by pointing at Action::is_action_successful() rather than
telling callers to write their own phase catch-all.

Stop hashing 5.3GB of dead sources on every `flyte run` (#1)

`flyte run examples/human-approval/task.py` spent 11.7s of a 13.9s startup
inside `Image._get_hash_digest()`, reading every file under
`../flyte-sdk/rs_controller/target/` before it could ask the registry whether
the image already existed.

Two independent causes, both fixed here.

The ignore file was a no-op for the tag hash. The SDK consumes the ignore list
through two paths, and only one accepts an arbitrary filename: the build-context
upload reads the DockerIgnore layer's path directly, but `_get_hash_digest`
builds a `DockerfileIgnore(<dir of that path>)`, and that class loads only
`<dir>/.dockerignore` and only matches paths underneath `<dir>`. Our
`rust.dockerignore`, shipped inside the package, failed both conditions, so its
matcher was None and nothing was excluded -- not `target/`, and not `*.py`
either. That second omission meant editing `task.py` or refreshing
`interface_gen.py` changed the image tag and forced a full remote Rust rebuild.

Add `/.dockerignore` at the workspace root -- the one name and location the hash
honours -- and prefer it over the packaged copy, which stays as a template.

`rs_controller` was also already dead weight. 170eabe moved `flyte_core` to a
git dependency, so nothing path-depends on that checkout; cargo never looked at
the 5.3GB being hashed and uploaded. Drop it from the image layers, the task
plumbing, all four example launchers, docker/Dockerfile and build-image.sh.

Add two warnings so this cannot stall silently again: one when no usable root
`.dockerignore` is found, one naming any copied folder whose `target/` the hash
will walk regardless.

Warm `flyte run`: 15.15s -> 1.76s (tag hash 11.72s -> 0.004s, local CPU
9.2s -> 0.56s). Verified across all four examples that `.rs` edits still change
the tag and `.py` edits no longer do, and that the worker image builds without
the rs_controller context.

Add PyPI and crates.io release workflows

Two independent release trains, tagged `py-v*` and `rs-v*`.

The packages are deliberately not version-locked. What couples the launcher to
the worker is the descriptor contract (`flyte_interface_version`), which is
already explicit and checked at runtime with a clear error naming both sides.
Matching version numbers would add nothing on top of that check while forcing
empty releases on whichever half did not change. docs/releasing.md records the
reasoning, including the one unversioned contract (the worker's argument list)
that should be treated as a descriptor bump when it changes.

release-python.yml lints, builds sdist + wheel, checks the tag against
pyproject.toml, asserts rust.dockerignore is inside both artifacts, installs the
wheel into a clean venv and imports it, then uploads via PyPI Trusted Publishing
(no stored token). The dockerignore assertion guards the regression fixed in #1:
that file is force-included and is not a .py file, so packaging changes can drop
it silently, and a wheel without it means multi-GB contexts and a rebuild per
run.

release-rust.yml runs clippy and the test suite, checks the tag against the
workspace version, dry-run publishes both crates, then publishes flyte-macros
before flyte.

Publishing prerequisites, all verified with `cargo publish --dry-run`:
- add `repository` metadata to both crates;
- give the `flyte-macros` path dependency a version requirement, since crates.io
  strips `path` and resolves from the registry.

rejects those. The dry-run step fails with that exact error rather than letting

Examples depend on the published flyte crate

With `flyte` 0.1.0 on crates.io, the examples can be what a user would actually
write. Each manifest now says `flyte = "0.1"` with literal versions instead of
workspace inheritance and a path dependency, and each task.py has lost its last
repo-specific argument. A user can copy an example directory out of the tree and
it builds.

That standalone property is not cosmetic -- it is what lets the worker image
build from the example directory alone rather than from a copy of the whole
workspace, which is smaller, faster, and no longer perturbed by unrelated crates.

`[patch.crates-io]` in the root manifest keeps the dev loop honest: in-workspace
builds redirect `flyte` to crates/flyte, so `cargo build` and `cargo test` still
exercise the working tree even though the manifests name a released version. The
patch does not apply when the directory is built on its own, which is exactly the
distinction wanted.

Two things had to be fixed for the crate-only context to be correct:

find_binary now walks up from the crate instead of looking in one fixed place.
Dropping `workspace=` moved the search to crate_dir/target, but a workspace
member builds into the *workspace root's* target/ -- so the binary was never
found, and every example silently fell back to its bundled interface_gen.py.
That would have quietly given up the guarantee that the Rust signature is what
gets launched: a renamed parameter would no longer be caught. The walk is
bounded at the enclosing repository so a miss cannot match an unrelated binary
somewhere up the filesystem. Verified the refresh works by corrupting a bundled
descriptor and watching it get rewritten from the binary.

Each example also gets its own .dockerignore. The build-context root moved from
the workspace to the crate, and the SDK's tag hash only honours an ignore file
named .dockerignore at that root -- without one, editing task.py would mint a new
image tag and rebuild the worker on every run.

Verified: cargo build/test/clippy clean; a standalone copy of an example builds
against the registry crate; all four launchers resolve their interface from the
binary with no warnings; editing task.py, interface_gen.py or a README leaves the
tag alone while editing main.rs or Cargo.toml changes it; and `flyte run
examples/hello-trace/task.py my_task --x 21 --label demo` reaches
ACTION_PHASE_SUCCEEDED with the image built from the crate directory alone.
